claims.text: The two-phase coexistence method can be used to calculate the melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The method directly simulates a solid-liquid interface.
A two-phase coexistence simulation can yield the melting temperature.
A two-phase coexistence simulation can yield the latent heat and the entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
A two-phase coexistence simulation can yield the volume change at melting.
The two-phase coexistence method avoids full thermodynamic integration of free energies.
Full ab initio thermodynamic integration is more computationally expensive than the proposed two-phase approach.
The proposed calculation uses ab initio molecular dynamics for a system containing solid and liquid regions under constant pressure and temperature.
A sufficiently large simulation cell allows stabilization of the solid-liquid interface.
The solid-liquid interface mediates phase equilibrium.
Intrinsic interface dynamics enable the two-phase system to equilibrate at the melting temperature.
The enthalpy difference between the coexisting phases can be used to infer the latent heat of fusion.
The density difference between the coexisting phases can be used to infer the volume change at melting.
The two-phase method should predict a melting temperature close to that obtained from full ab initio free-energy calculations.
Full ab initio free-energy calculations using thermodynamic integration are accurate but computationally expensive.
The accuracy of the two-phase method may decline when interface kinetics are extremely slow.
The accuracy of the two-phase method may decline when finite-size effects dominate.
Calculated melting properties may be sensitive to simulation-cell size, interface fluctuations, and errors in the DFT approximation.
